title: RAM capacity showing less than installed

question_tree.question: Is this a brand new RAM stick you just added, or one that was already working fine before?

options.answer: Brand new stick

next.question: Did you check if your motherboard (the main circuit board that connects all parts) is securely holding both sides of the stick until you heard a physical click?

options.answer: No, I might not have pushed it in all the way

next.text:
1. Turn off your PC completely, unplug the power cable, and open the side panel of your computer case.
2. Press down firmly on both ends of the new RAM stick until the plastic clips on the sides snap closed by themselves.
3. Plug the power back in and turn the PC on to check if Windows now detects the full amount.

options.answer: Yes, it is clicked in completely

next.text:
1. Press the Windows key, type 'msconfig', open System Configuration, go to the 'Boot' tab, and click 'Advanced options'.
2. Check if the box next to 'Maximum memory' is ticked — if it is, uncheck it, click OK, and restart your computer.
3. If that doesn't fix it, check your motherboard manufacturer's website to see if your BIOS (the basic system software running before Windows) needs an update to recognize newer RAM sizes.

options.answer: Old stick that used to work

next.question: Have you noticed any physical dust buildup or debris inside the RAM slot (the long connector where memory sits)?

options.answer: Yes, looks dusty

next.text:
1. Power down your PC, unplug it, and carefully remove the RAM stick from its slot.
2. Use a can of compressed air to gently blow out any dust or debris from inside the empty slot.
3. Wipe the gold pins of the RAM stick gently with a clean microfiber cloth before clicking it back into place.

options.answer: No, it looks clean

next.text:
1. Note whether only one specific stick is failing to show up or if Windows is showing hardware reservation limits.
2. One of your RAM sticks or the slot itself may have suffered permanent physical failure, so it's best to have a technician test the components individually with specialized hardware diagnostic tools.

title: Random crashes or Blue Screen errors

question_tree.question: Did you recently turn on an overclocking setting like XMP or DOCP in your BIOS (the low-level setup menu before Windows loads) to make your RAM run faster?

options.answer: Yes, I turned on XMP/DOCP recently

next.text:
1. Restart your PC and repeatedly press the Delete or F2 key to enter your BIOS settings screen.
2. Look for the XMP or DOCP profile option and turn it off or set it back to 'Default' or 'Auto'.
3. Save changes and exit — often, aggressive speed boosts cause instability if the RAM can't handle the rated speed reliably.

options.answer: No, I haven't changed any BIOS settings

next.question: Do you have more than one RAM stick installed in your computer right now?

options.answer: Yes, multiple sticks

next.text:
1. Power down your PC and take out all RAM sticks except for one single stick.
2. Turn on the PC and use it normally to see if the crashes stop; if it still crashes, swap that stick for the other one.
3. This process of elimination lets you find out if a single specific RAM stick has gone bad and needs replacement.

options.answer: No, just a single stick

next.text:
1. Click the Windows Start menu, type 'Windows Memory Diagnostic', and select it.
2. Choose 'Restart now and check for problems' and let your computer run the built-in scan while it reboots.
3. Once Windows turns back on, check the notification center for any reported memory hardware errors.

title: PC turns on but no display on monitor
keywords: monitor says no signal after hardware change

question_tree.question: Did this black screen happen immediately after you installed, moved, or cleaned your RAM sticks?

options.answer: Yes, right after touching the RAM

next.text:
1. Unplug the PC power cord completely from the wall outlet for safety.
2. Take out the RAM sticks and re-insert them, making sure you hear a distinct click from both the top and bottom retaining clips.
3. If your motherboard has four slots and you are using two sticks, ensure they are placed in the correct alternating slots (usually slot 2 and 4 counting away from the CPU) as recommended in your motherboard manual.

options.answer: No, it happened out of nowhere

next.question: Does your motherboard have small indicator lights near the RAM slots that stay lit up with a red or orange glow when you turn the PC on?

options.answer: Yes, a warning light is lit up

next.text:
1. Check the small text label next to the lit-up warning light — if it says 'DRAM', your computer is failing to communicate with your memory.
2. Unplug your PC, take out all RAM sticks, wipe their contacts gently, and plug back just one stick in the primary slot to see if the light goes away.

options.answer: No / I don't see any warning lights

next.text:
1. Note down whether your PC makes any unusual pattern of short or long beep sounds when you press the power button.
2. A persistent no-display issue tied to memory detection failure can mean a damaged motherboard slot or CPU pin issue, which requires physical inspection by a professional repair technician.

title: PC keeps restarting in a continuous loop
keywords: pc turns on and off repeatedly
restarts on its own before loading windows

question_tree.question: Does the computer manage to show the Windows login screen before restarting, or does it restart continuously before any picture appears?

options.answer: Restarts continuously before showing any picture

next.text:
1. Unplug the power cable and open your PC case.
2. Remove all RAM sticks from the motherboard completely.
3. Put back only a single stick of RAM firmly into the second slot away from the processor, then try turning the system back on to break the loop.

options.answer: It reaches Windows or the loading logo first, then restarts

next.question: Have you installed any new software updates or hardware drivers right before this reboot loop started?

options.answer: Yes, installed updates or drivers

next.text:
1. Turn your PC on and off manually three times in a row during startup to force Windows into the Automatic Repair menu.
2. Navigate to Advanced Options > Troubleshoot > Advanced Options > Startup Settings and click Restart.
3. Press F4 when prompted to boot into Safe Mode, then uninstall the recent driver or program causing the stability failure.

options.answer: No, nothing new was installed

next.text:
1. Shut down the system completely and unplug it from the wall socket.
2. Locate the coin-sized silver battery (CMOS battery) on your motherboard, take it out gently for 5 minutes, and put it back in.
3. This resets your BIOS and memory timings back to factory safety defaults, stopping instability loops caused by corrupted configuration settings.

title: Startup warning beeps or motherboard error light

question_tree.question: When you turn on the computer, do you hear a repeating pattern of specific beep sounds (like 3 short beeps or a long beep)?

options.answer: Yes, hearing specific beep codes

next.text:
1. Count the exact number and length of the beeps (e.g., 3 short beeps is a classic memory error code on most motherboards).
2. Look up your motherboard brand name online along with the beep pattern to confirm it points to a RAM error.
3. Reseat your RAM sticks firmly into their slots to clear the connection fault triggering the audio alarm.

options.answer: No beeps, but there is a steady error light on the board

next.question: Is the glowing light next to the label that says 'DRAM' or 'MEM_OK'?

options.answer: Yes, it is next to DRAM

next.text:
1. Power down your system and locate the 'MEM_OK' button if your motherboard has one near the RAM slots.
2. Press and hold that button for 3 seconds until an LED starts blinking; the motherboard will automatically test and fix safe memory compatibility settings for you.
3. If there is no button, take out your RAM sticks and test them one by one in different slots.

options.answer: No, the light is next to CPU or BOOT instead

next.text:
1. Record a short video of the motherboard indicator lights and startup behavior so you can show it to a hardware technician.
2. Since the error points away from RAM toward core processor or boot systems, professional diagnostic equipment is required to safely test and swap those expensive parts.
